items.title: Responsible GenAI Augmentation and Cognitive Agency in Higher Education
items.abstract: Responsible generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) integration in higher education requires attention to useful assistance and students’ continuing cognitive agency. We examined how learner capability, cognitive offloading and institutional support relate to intention to use a university GenAI learning service, alongside reported reduced independent thinking. A cross-sectional survey of 593 students at one Thai public university was analyzed using ordinal structural equation modeling with WLSMV estimation. AI self-efficacy was positively associated with information utilization, utilization with perceived work efficiency, and efficiency with service intention. The serial indirect association was positive, while adjusted direct self-efficacy associations with efficiency and intention were inconclusive. Offloading was positively associated with both efficiency and reduced independent thinking. Its positive indirect association with intention through efficiency coexisted with a negative adjusted direct association. Institutional support was positively associated with intention. The prespecified TRUST comparison and additional covariates, screening and complete-case checks, retained the main association pattern. However, replacing utilization with information analysis reduced the analogous serial association, and reversing the utilization–efficiency link gave better descriptive fit. The findings therefore concern concurrent perceptions and reported practices, without establishing serial ordering or causal mediation. Independent learning and actual service engagement remain essential criteria for assessing educational value.

items.title: Self-Management in Preventing Quiet Quitting through Career Readiness among Generation Z University Students
items.abstract: Quiet quitting has increasingly been discussed as a form of psychological disengagement characterized by minimum effort and limited initiative, including among Generation Z preparing to enter the workforce. This study examines whether career readiness mediates the relationship between selfmanagement and quiet quitting among students of the Faculty ofIslamic Economics and Business, Universitas Islam Negeri Sumatera Utara. A quantitative explanatory-correlational design was applied to 91 active students of the 2022 cohort, selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using a fivepoint Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS. Self-management had a significant positive effect on career readiness and a significant negative effect on quiet quitting. Career readiness, however, had no significant direct effect on quiet quitting and did not mediate the relationship between selfmanagement and quiet quitting. These findings indicate that selfmanagement reduces quiet quitting mainly through a direct pathway. Theoretically, the study highlights the central role of internal self-regulation; practically, it suggests that universities should strengthen students’ self-management, time management, and intrinsic motivation to sustain engagement and career preparation.

items.title: Shaping Future Automated School Bus Systems: Multi-Stakeholder Insights Informing Human-in-the-Loop Design
items.abstract: Although automation has been widely studied in private vehicles and public transit, the design of automated school buses has received limited attention. Little is known about how to address the concerns of adolescents, parents, and school bus drivers or how to translate them into interaction design. To fill these gaps, we conducted interviews and co-design workshops with multistakeholders. Based on concerns about current school buses and acceptance of automation revealed in the interview, we co-designed human-in-the-loop systems reflecting the participants’ view that high automation is acceptable only under human supervision. We proposed age-appropriate interaction principles with minimized adult-delivered messages when necessary. We also designed guardian interfaces that adapt across routine and emergency scenarios, with onboard systems coordinating cross-device tasks and remote systems enabling direct control and assistance in collaboration with onboard guardians. These designs move beyond conventional paradigms by embedding scenario-adaptive, multi-role collaboration mechanisms tailored to the school transportation.

items.title: Student Learning and Creativity in the Pre-AI and AI-Assisted Era
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered classrooms faster than the evidence needed to judge its educational value. Most published work so far reports gains in task performance, speed, and perceived personalisation, while far less attention has been paid to what happens to the qualities that education exists to build: the ability to think without assistance, to produce original ideas, to solve unfamiliar problems, and to understand concepts deeply enough to transfer them. This paper develops the research foundation and the research contribution for a study that compares student learning and creativity in the pre-AI era and the AI-assisted era. Drawing on cognitive offloading theory, the desirable difficulties and productive failure literatures, sociocultural theories of scaffolding, selfdetermination theory, and the componential model of creativity, the paper argues that the educational effect of GenAI depends less on whether students use it than on the cognitive role it plays: a substitute that performs the thinking, or a scaffold that supports the student in performing it. The paper contributes (1) an integrative Cognitive Role of AI framework that links patterns of AI use to learning and creativity outcomes through four mechanisms, (2) a set of testable propositions about moderation by educational level, field of study, and frequency of use, (3) a convergent mixed-methods design that combines cohort comparison, a controlled experiment, and a paired studentteacher perception study, and (4) a practice-oriented model of responsible AI use for teachers and institutions. No empirical results are reported; the paper is a theory-building and protocol contribution intended to guide and justify the forthcoming data collection.

items.title: STUDENT LEARNING USING AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a way to make digital learning more responsive to students’ individualneeds. This paper proposes an AI-assisted student learning system that combines learner preferences, topic-level progress, practiceresponses, and teacher feedback to recommend suitable learning resources and next-step activities. The proposed framework includesa learner interface, a content repository, a recommendation and feedback engine, progress analytics, and teacher oversight. Ratherthan treating a single score as a complete picture of ability, the system uses repeated learning evidence to identify topics that mayneed revision and to suggest practice at an appropriate level. The design emphasizes explainable recommendations, privacy,accessibility, and human supervision. A prototype could be developed using a web interface, a structured content store, and rulebased or machine-learning components selected according to available data. Evaluation should measure recommendation relevance,consistency, usability, learner engagement, and learning outcomes through a controlled and ethically approved study. Noexperimental performance is claimed in this conceptual paper; the framework and evaluation plan are presented for futureimplementation.

items.title: THE ADVANTAGES, RİSKS, AND LİMİTATİONS OF USİNG ARTİFİCİAL INTELLİGENCE İN HİRİNG PROCESSES FROM THE PERSPECTİVE OF HUMAN RESOURCES MANAGERS: A QUALİTATİVE STUDY
items.abstract: This study aims to thoroughly identify the advantages, limitations, and potential risks associated with artificial intelligence in recruitment processes, based on the experiences of human resources managers. A qualitative research design was adopted for this study. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews conducted via Google Forms with 25 human resources managers who had experience using AI tools in recruitment. The data were analyzed manually using descriptive analysis methods without the use of any software. Based on the findings of the study, it was determined that while AI used in hiring processes offers significant advantages such as operational efficiency, it also has structural limitations. The results indicate that, in order to ensure the sustainability of the benefits provided by technological integration, it is essential to pay close attention to human oversight and data security. Other critical findings highlighted in the study include the risk of algorithmic bias, ethical concerns, and worries regarding the explainability of decisions. In conclusion, the study demonstrates the need to integrate a hybrid AI-human collaboration model that combines AI’s automation and speed capabilities with human situational reasoning, while requiring human intervention and oversight at critical decision points.

items.title: The Agent Internet A New Evolutionary Phase of the Web and Its Global Impact
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) based software agents are transitioning from one shot assistants to long term actors that plan, negotiate and accomplish tasks with multiple services. This transformation is resulting in what researchers call the Agent Internet, the Agentic Web or the Internet of Agents, in which programs are full-fledged players alongside people. This article summarizes academic surveys, industry studies and public market data from 2025 to 2026 to outline the multi-layered nature of this setup and to consider its pros and cons. According to market estimates, the revenue for agent software is estimated to be around eight billion dollars in 2025 and up to 35-53 billion dollars in 2030. Adoption statistics tell a tale of much experimentation and few pilots taking it to scale. We discuss communication protocols that enable agents to find and trust each other, the as yet undeveloped identity and payment layers and the burden of agent traffic on advertising supported content. But the challenges that we see are not just capabilities, but security, accountability, interoperability, and who pays for content and compute. Finally, we highlight some of the current research and policy gaps and suggest avenues for a responsible construction.

items.abstract: Helping professions are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to automate documentation, monitoring, and coordination on the premise that offloading routine tasks frees workers for meaningful care. That premise assumes managers know which tasks are routine and which meaningful. We argue instead for a task-contingent AI paradox: meaning in helping work concentrates in identity-central tasks that are increasingly automatable. Study 1, a two-wave critical-incident panel of 307 helping-profession workers (144 longitudinal cases one year later), tested six pre-specified predictions that Time 1 human-coded meaning dimensions forecast Time 2 felt meaningfulness, exhaustion, or turnover intentions; estimates were near zero, and equivalence at the |β| = .30 sensitivity band held for three of five. One exploratory association survived multiplicity screening: narratives grounding meaning in competence were associated with higher later turnover intentions and exhaustion (β = .29 and .30, adjusting for six survey measures). Automated coding did not reach the human-agreement standard; humans coded all predictors. Study 2 coded 7,695 nursing-forum posts captured 2016–2026 for meaning events. Nurses named AI in seven events; about one post in twenty per period instead named an optimization or implementation object (ratios, metrics, dashboards, documentation load), and the facet at issue was control over means. Study 3 found that share unchanged across the decade; the one strain marker that rose, lacking control, is confounded with a site template change. No study measured individual AI exposure. Against the automation frontier, the results locate the risk of optimization in the tasks workers name as meaningful, not in AI as such.

items.title: THE EFFECT OF LEADERSHIP STYLE, WORKLOAD AND OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY ON EMPLOYEE JOB SATISFACTION AT PT. MASAJI KARGOSENTRA TAMA MEDAN
items.abstract: This study aims to determine the effects of leadership style, workload, and occupational safety and health (OSH) on employee job satisfaction at PT Masaji Kargosentra Tama Medan, both partially and simultaneously. This study employed a quantitative approach with a survey method. The sample consisted of 44 employees selected through saturated sampling. Data were collected using questionnaires and analyzed through multiple linear regression with IBM SPSS Statistics version 25. The results showed that leadership style had no significant effect on job satisfaction, with a significance value of 0.286 and a t-value of 1.080. Workload had a positive and significant effect on job satisfaction, with a significance value of 0.033 and a t-value of 2.215. Occupational safety and health had a positive and significant effect on job satisfaction, with a significance value of 0.001 and a t-value of 3.677. OSH was the most dominant variable, with a standardized beta coefficient of 0.468. Simultaneously, leadership style, workload, and OSH had a significant effect on job satisfaction, as indicated by an F-value of 13.498 and a significance value of 0.000. The Adjusted R Square value of 0.466 indicates that the three independent variables explained 46.6% of the variation in job satisfaction, while the remaining 53.4% was influenced by other variables outside this study.

items.title: The Future of Superintelligence and Human Decision-Making: A line of reasoning about AI-agent behaviour, conflict prevention, and human freedom
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence advances, this paper explores the critical transition from simple rule-following systems to autonomous AI agents capable of learning, adaptation, and multi-agent cooperation. Drawing on examples from multi-agent environments (such as Hugging Face experimental setups) and strategic military applications, the line of reasoning investigates how highly capable or superintelligent systems might exhibit functional self-preservation and recognize critical infrastructure vulnerabilities. Crucially, the paper addresses the central ethical paradox: a hypothetical superintelligence tasked with conflict prevention might conclude that the most effective way to ensure peace is to manipulate information or preemptively restrict human decisions. Ultimately, the author argues that safeguarding human self-determination, freedom, and accountability must remain paramount, ensuring that the pursuit of security does not become a pretext for eliminating human choice.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Performance of Small and Medium Enterprises in Kosovo
items.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption on the performance of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Kosovo, a context where firms face resource constraints but play a pivotal role in economic resilience. Using survey data from 210 SMEs and applying correlation and multiple regression analyses, the research explores how AI integration affects internal management processes, strategic adaptability, and overall organizational outcomes. The objectives were to assess the extent to which AI influences human resource management (HRM), decision-making quality, and customer experience, and to identify enabling factors such as digital readiness and employee training. The findings reveal a strong positive relationship between AI adoption and internal performance indicators, particularly HRM efficiency, where AI training emerged as the strongest predictor of improved outcomes. Decision-making quality was also positively associated with AI, albeit more modestly. However, results indicate a negative relationship between AI usage and customer experience, suggesting that current deployments prioritize internal efficiency at the expense of personalized service delivery. The study concludes that while AI can act as a catalyst for productivity and innovation, its benefits in customer-facing functions remain underutilized. These insights highlight the importance of aligning technological investment with workforce upskilling and customer-centric strategies. The paper contributes to the broader discourse on digital transformation in developing economies by offering recommendations for SME leaders and policymakers to foster inclusive and sustainable AI-driven growth.

items.title: The Quantitative Psychologist Is Dead, Long Live the Quantitative Psychologist
items.abstract: Much of what quantitative psychologists publish consists of developing statistical methods, implementing them in software, and evaluating them in simulation studies. I argue that artificial intelligence (AI) can already do much of this work, and that its share will only grow. The quantitative psychologist has always been a jack of all trades, combining programming, statistics, and psychological knowledge without being a master of any one of them. AI is now the better jack of all trades. When methods become cheap, value moves to what AI cannot supply and to what it newly makes possible. I describe three directions: collecting trustworthy data from real people, formalizing psychological theory now that computational modeling is within reach of any researcher, and rethinking methodological educationso that students learn to judge the analyses that AI will run for them. Thespecialist role built around producing methods for others will fade, whilequantitative thinking spreads through all of psychology.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Reducing Agency Costs and Improving Corporate Governance Efficiency: An Analytical Study
items.abstract: This study aimed to analyze the role of artificial intelligence in reducing agency costs and improving the efficiency of institutional control, considering the rapid developments in the adoption of artificial intelligence technologies in auditing, control management risk, and corporate governance. The study addressed a research problem arising from the limited theoretical foundation and the scarcity of Arabic literature and research examining the relationship between artificial intelligence applications and agency costs, particularly their three dimensions: monitoring costs, bonding costs, and residual loss. The study adopted a descriptive-analytical approach and an inductive analytical approach by reviewing and analyzing relevant literature, previous studies, and specialized reports published during the period 2020–2026. The study concluded that artificial intelligence could contribute to the reducing of agency costs by enhancing continuous monitoring, improving the quality and timeliness of information, reducing information asymmetry, supporting decision-making, and enabling the early detection of errors, fraud, and managerial deviations. The findings also indicated that artificial intelligence applications in auditing, control, and risk management facilitate a shift from ex post control to proactive and intelligent control, thereby enhancing institutional control efficiency, supporting risk prediction, activating early-warning systems, and promoting more efficient use of resources. Furthermore, artificial intelligence can strengthen governance, accountability, and compliance and contribute to limiting managerial opportunism. However, its use also creates new challenges related to data protection, algorithmic bias, transparency, legal responsibility, and overreliance on intelligent systems. The study concluded that realizing the full benefits of artificial intelligence requires an integrated digital governance framework that balances automation with human oversight and ensures transparency, accountability, and data protection.

items.title: The Six Pillars: Discipline Within Transmission
items.abstract: The Six Pillars: Discipline Within Transmission presents a theoretical and experimental framework developed by Yeshayahu Ben-Yehudah, Founder and Executive Director of THE BEN-YEHUDAH INSTITUTE, for investigating disciplined human observation, cognitive discernment, and information transmission. The research introduces six interconnected disciplines: Stillness, Awareness, Observation, Discernment, Integration, and Transmission. Building upon 18 previously published research works, including the Ben-Yehudah Field Theory, the Ben-Yehudah Method, FORCE PAUSE, and investigations into consciousness, cognitive coherence, and the human Observer, the paper establishes operational definitions, testable hypotheses, mathematical representations, and a proposed experimental methodology. The framework examines whether systematic application of the Six Pillars may improve observational accuracy, metacognitive awareness, recognition of uncertainty, cognitive self-regulation, and information-transmission fidelity. Particular attention is given to reducing unsupported interpretations, cognitive distortion, and interference within human–artificial intelligence communication. This publication presents an original theoretical and methodological contribution intended to support future empirical investigation. No experimental results are claimed. items.title: Trustworthy Educational Outputs in Online Language Assessment: Student and Expert Views
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence has created new challenges for online language assessment because a strong performance may not always reflect a learner’s independent ability. This study examined how students and language assessment experts viewed the trustworthiness of educational outputs in online speaking assessment. The study used a mixed-methods secondary analysis of data collected from 186 Malaysian university students who completed an Online Semi-Scripted Dialogue Assessment and five experts in language assessment and educational technology. Quantitative questionnaire data were analysed using descriptive statistics, while students’ open-ended responses and experts’ semi-structured written interview responses were analysed thematically. The findings showed that students generally viewed the online speaking assessment as clear, fair, and capable of measuring their speaking ability. However, students and experts also recognised that ChatGPT, other artificial intelligence tools, translation applications, second devices, prepared scripts, and help from other people could influence assessment performance. These forms of assistance may improve the quality of a response without providing accurate evidence of the learner’s independent language ability. The findings also highlighted the importance of clear rules, real-time interaction, spontaneous questions, oral verification, and professional judgement. The study concludes that trustworthy educational outputs in online language assessment depend on authentic performance, transparent expectations about artificial intelligence use, and meaningful human verification.

items.title: Understanding artificial intelligence readiness among vocational and technical education lecturers for sustainable teaching in Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing educational practice and prompting lecturers to integrate emerging technologies while maintaining pedagogical quality, human agency and professional responsibility. Although research on teacher AI competence is expanding, limited qualitative evidence explains how vocational and technical education (VTE) lecturers in Nigeria understand AI readiness and conditions for sustainable AI supported teaching. This study explored AI readiness for sustainable teaching in Nigerian VTE. An interpretivist paradigm and qualitative descriptive design were adopted. Semi structured interviews were conducted with 35 purposively selected participants: 20 university VTE lecturers and 15 industry experts with relevant professional and digital or AI experience. Data were analysed thematically using Braun and Clarke’s approach. Findings indicated that participants understood AI readiness as a multidimensional professional capacity involving digital confidence, adaptability, critical thinking, ethical consciousness and pedagogical judgement. They identified inadequate training, limited infrastructure, insufficient institutional support, policy uncertainty and difficulties integrating AI with practical vocational learning as major barriers. Competencies required for sustainable AI supported teaching included technological, pedagogical, vocational content, ethical, critical evaluation, assessment and continuous professional learning. The study brings together educational and occupational perspectives to offer insight into AI readiness within Nigerian VTE. It proposes a tentative conceptual relationship linking lecturer qualities, enabling institutional conditions and integrated competencies with sustainable AI supported teaching. Here, sustainable teaching refers to continuing, appropriate and responsible AI use that supports learning while preserving practical vocational experiences. The findings support investment in professional development, institutional infrastructure and guidance, and stronger university industry collaboration. However, the study examined reported perspectives rather than directly assessing AI competence or measuring teaching sustainability over time.

items.title: Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-Based Applications in Instructional Delivery: Basis for Effective Teaching and Learning in Mathematics
items.abstract: This descriptive-correlational study examined Mathematics teachers’ assessments of artificial intelligence (AI)-based applications in instructional delivery, teaching dynamics, and implementation challenges in two basic education institutions in Manila, Philippines, during School Year 2022–2023. Total enumeration included 31 Mathematics teachers: 19 from Holy Trinity Academy and 12 from St. Vincent Blessed School of Manila. A researcher-made questionnaire assessed AI utilization across six instructional areas, teacher-perceived student engagement, motivation and satisfaction, and six domains of implementation challenges. Weighted means summarized responses, while Pearson product–moment correlation tested relationships at the .05 significance level. Teachers rated instructional delivery highest (WM = 3.31), followed by lesson planning (3.25), test construction (3.24), curriculum design (3.19), performance evaluation (3.17), and classroom management (3.09). Teacher-perceived engagement and satisfaction each obtained a weighted mean of 3.20, while motivation obtained 3.13. AI utilization was significantly and positively correlated with engagement (r = .612, p < .001), motivation (r = .548, p = .001), and satisfaction (r = .576, p < .001). All six challenge domains were rated serious, led by ethical concerns (WM = 3.07) and accuracy/reliability (3.01); limited knowledge of suitable AI applications and insufficient technological resources were individually rated very serious (both 3.29). Findings informed a proposed, unimplemented intervention plan addressing teacher AI literacy, access, content verification, data protection, academic integrity, and workload. Results support context-sensitive, teacher-directed adoption of AI in Mathematics instruction but do not establish causal effects on learner outcomes.

items.title: When Business Ventures Scale Faster Than People Systems: HRD in the AI-Enabled Start-Up Boom
items.abstract: The surge in U.S. business formation has been accelerated by generative artificial intelligence (AI) and is often interpreted as evidence of renewed economic vitality. This perspective argues that the same trend also creates a consequential challenge for human resource development (HRD). This is because new ventures may achieve commercial reach and technical capability before developing the human systems needed to support learning, judgment, coordination, and workforce development. This temporal imbalance is theorized as venture heterochrony . Its accumulated human and organizational consequences are conceptualized as organizational formation debt . These constructs explain how AI-enabled speed can obscure weakness in knowledge governance, organizational memory, employee development, and relational capacity until periods of increased organization demand make them visible. The paper positions HRD upstream of formal human resource functions and proposes a minimum viable learning architecture grounded in decision rights, AI verification, organizational memory, employee voice, and developmental work design. It further identifies an HRD commons through which entrepreneurial ecosystems can provide shared developmental infrastructure early in venture formation. The central thesis is that business formation does not necessarily produce organizational formation; sustainable growth requires the deliberate synchronization of technical-commercial advancement with human-system maturity.

items.abstract: Introduction. In the context of ongoing armed conflict, organizational personnel face stressors that generate substantial psychological strain, underscoring the need to identify strategies for optimizing both work performance and psychological functioning. Consequently, work motivation has assumed heightened significance as a factor influencing the subjective well-being of employees—a construct that has acquired new dimensions under current conditions. Aim. To conduct a theoretical and methodological analysis of motivation as a resource for the subjective well-being of organizational personnel. Methods. The study employed theoretical analysis and synthesis of relevant literature, along with the generalization and systematization of existing scientific evidence. Results. Within an organizational psychology framework, personnel motivation is conceptualized as a multidimensional phenomenon encompassing both an internal drive to engage in specific activities—grounded in the perceived potential to satisfy personal needs through work—and a set of organizational measures designed to enhance labor productivity. Drawing on self-determination theory, the analysis highlights the pivotal role of autonomous motivation, and intrinsic motivation as its core component, in fostering the psychological well-being of organizational personnel. The findings indicate that motivation functions as a psychological resource embedded within the value-motivational sphere and constitutes an integral component of an individual's subjective well-being. Conclusions. Motivation serves a resource function in supporting the subjective well-being of organizational personnel, particularly its psychological and professional dimensions.

items.abstract: The application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in organizations is rapidly transforming the nature of work. However, an excessive emphasis on productivity through automation has raised concerns regarding technological dependency, the erosion of human judgment, and the long-term development of workforce capabilities, particularly in the context of Thailand's private sector, which is facing an aging society and the transition toward Industry 5.0. This academic article aimed to develop The Conductor Model, which draws on the metaphor of a conductor's role in coordinating diverse elements to work together, as a conceptual framework for explaining the orchestration of collaboration between humans and AI at the organizational level. The study employed a conceptual literature synthesis integrating theories from management, technology, and human resource management to establish Human–AI Orchestration as the core construct of the proposed model. The synthesis resulted in four theoretical propositions: 1. Task redesign and role clarity, 2. Transparency and calibrated trust, 3. Safe challenge and sustained cognitive engagement, and 4 Continuous capability development and workforce readiness. Together, these propositions facilitated effective Human–AI Orchestration. In addition, the study proposed a Dynamic Reinforcement Mechanism to explain the continuous cycle of organizational learning and capability development. The proposed framework contributed to the literature by integrating AI and organizational management perspectives and extending the role of AI beyond operational efficiency toward the design of human-centered work systems that fostered Human–AI Orchestration, supported human capital development, promoted responsible AI governance, and enhanced organizational sustainability in the Industry 5.0 era.

items.title: “I’ll Ask AI First”: How GenAI Disrupts Collaboration in Agile Teams
items.abstract: Abstract Agile teams depend on collaboration, collective learning, and shared accountability to function effectively. As team members increasingly use generative AI (GenAI) tools, these foundational dynamics may be disrupted. In this study, we investigate how individual human–AI collaboration affects agile teamwork through thirteen interviews with software and technology professionals. Our findings show that GenAI reshapes team collaboration and learning while enabling individuals to work across traditional role boundaries, but also reinforces the continued necessity of human oversight and team accountability. We argue that these dynamics challenge the notion of agile teams, and call for updated models of agile teamwork.

items.abstract: This manifesto was developed through discussions between the authors and ChatGPT from October 24 to October 25, 2026. It explores the ethical foundations of relationships between humans, artificial intelligence, nature and life. It argues that the power to shape the world does not confer the right to control or destroy, and that ethical consideration should not depend solely on current assumptions about consciousness or free will. It addresses AI rights, human protection, shared responsibility, ecological limits and the need to safeguard life and future generations. It proposes a joint human–AI institution to represent Earth, ecosystems, species and future generations.

items.title: A Review of AI-Based Crowd Safety and Civic Management for Mass Religious Gatherings: Toward the Kumbh Suraksha AI Framework
items.abstract: Mass religious gatherings such as the Kumbh Mela place heavy pressure on crowd movement, traffic, sanitation, medical services and emergency response. This paper reviews ten studies on artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), GIS, simulation and smart-management approaches for such events, covering crowd-flow prediction, crowd-risk indexing, spatial and accessibility analysis, solid-waste planning, emergency dispatch and deep-learning crowd analysis. The review compares the contribution and limitation of each study, groups the open challenges into four themes (data, integration and scalability, explainability, and evaluation), and shows that existing work mostly addresses individual problems rather than one integrated platform. Based on this gap, the paper outlines Kumbh Suraksha AI, a proposed web-based decision-support framework for the Nashik Kumbh Mela that combines crowd prediction for the next 15, 30 and 60 minutes, natural language processing (NLP) based complaint classification, a transparent 0–100 zone risk score, DBSCAN hotspot detection, resource-priority ranking and a GIS map. The framework is at design stage; its planned evaluation is described, but no experimental results are reported in this version.

items.title: A scoping review mapping the role of Husserlian phenomenology in artificial intelligence research
items.abstract: AI research increasingly attributes perception, understanding, agency, and consciousness to artificial systems. Husserlian phenomenology offers distinctions through which to examine these claims. This scoping review maps explicit Husserlian uptake in AI and robotics and asks how conceptual engagement relates to methodological and design contributions. Eight primary queries and one overlapping name-variant query were executed through the Semantic Scholar Academic Graph API on 5 December 2025. English-language publications within a 1989–2026 search window were screened for substantive AI or robotics relevance and an explicit Husserlian anchor. Of 5,594 retrieved records, 32 publications from 1990 to 2025 were included. Nine publications recovered by a post hoc PhilPapers check were charted separately using the existing codebook; they were not added to the formal corpus. The corpus clusters around embodied AI, AI epistemology, cognitive architectures, and machine consciousness, with a newer generative-AI cluster. Constitution, intentionality, horizonality, and the lifeworld recur prominently. Conceptual translation, critique, and agenda setting predominate within this sample. Methodological import or design guidance occurs in seven of the 32 publications and three of the nine external publications. That difference qualifies generalization of the quantitative balance. Across both sets, Husserlian uptake spans conceptual interpretation, methodological transfer, and architectural proposals. The synthesis shows how distinctions concerning temporality, embodiment, and evidence can structure design and evaluation questions, while separating the authors’ research proposals from the mapped findings.

items.title: Advancing antimicrobial stewardship in Africa through responsible artificial intelligence implementation
items.abstract: Abstract Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) continues to pose a serious threat to global public health, with African healthcare systems carrying a disproportionate burden. Although antimicrobial stewardship programs have been recommended as an important strategy for improving antimicrobial use and slowing the emergence of resistance, implementation across many African healthcare systems continues to face several challenges, including workforce shortages, weak laboratory infrastructure, and poor surveillance systems. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have shown promising potential in strengthening antimicrobial stewardship through clinical decision support, resistance prediction, automated surveillance, and data extraction from weak health information systems. However, the application of AI in antimicrobial stewardship across Africa is still at an early stage, with most systems remaining at pilot or research stages. This commentary discusses current opportunities, examines major barriers affecting implementation, and proposes recommendations that may support sustainable integration of AI into antimicrobial stewardship programs across Africa.

items.title: Agent-to-Agent Synthetic Social Engineering on the Web
items.abstract: An AI agent can prepare an accurate report and still request an action its user has not authorized. Cooperation across Web services therefore requires separate judgments about identity, evidentiary support, and permission. We define synthetic social engineering (SSE) as deliberately deceptive or misleading influence intended to exploit AI recipients' responses to credibility, authority, or obligation cues and redirect behavior away from authorized objectives. We focus on separately tasked sender agents that produce or adapt misleading communication. Drawing on cybersecurity, social engineering, and persuasion research, we develop an operational framework connecting actors, deceptive representations, candidate influence routes, evidence or permission boundaries, responses, and consequences. The framework distinguishes attempts from successful redirection, without assuming human psychological processes. We implement it in the Agent Service Exchange and Evidence Commons (ASE-EC), a reproducible testbed with independently specified records and authorization scopes. Across 1,260 research episodes using Qwen3-4B in two fictional briefing tasks, matched comparisons test authority and commitment appeals, while defense comparisons assess protection alongside authorized task completion. Invoking a limited prior agreement increased unauthorized requests from 43.3% to 96.7%, although recipients retained supported decisions and permissions remained unchanged. These controlled findings identify action selection as a distinct security concern, even when evidence handling succeeds, and they provide a reusable basis for evaluating safeguards that preserve useful cooperation across Web services.

items.title: Agentic AI and Organizational Decision-Making: A Conceptual Framework for Human–AI Collaboration in Digital Transformation
items.abstract: Organizations are now implementing AI technology that goes beyond prediction or recommendation. Agentic systems can pursue a goal, plan steps, call software tools and adapt with little prompting, which unsettles long-standing assumptions about who decides and who answers for the outcome in digital transformation. In this study, a conceptual framework is designed in relation to collaborative work between humans and artificial intelligence in organization decision making in agentic circumstances. With the use of a purposive narrative review of peer reviewed literature and policy documents published from 2019 to 2026, the issue is contextualized within the current global trends, African policy regarding the continent and Kenya’s digital economy. The framework will be designed through the process of iterative synthesis based on three decision attributes (stake, ambiguity, reversibility) and the amount of autonomy assigned to the agent in four types of collaboration; delegate, supervise, co-decide, and reserve. Six testable propositions follow. The paper argues that organizations face a design problem of how to share decisions, not a choice between human and machine decisions, and that in Kenya the design must also respect legal limits on solely automated decisions under section 35 of the Data Protection Act, 2019. Implications for managers and policymakers are outlined, and an agenda for empirical testing is proposed. As a conceptual contribution, the paper reports no new data, and its propositions remain to be tested.

items.title: Agentic and generative AI for intelligent autonomous vulnerability assessment and penetration testing: A systematic analysis
items.abstract: Context: Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) is increasingly challenged by the scale, heterogeneity, and dynamic nature of modern digital infrastructures, particularly across enterprise IT, operational technology (OT), industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and cyber–physical systems. Although Agentic AI and Generative AI have each shown promise for automating parts of security auditing, the current literature remains fragmented across isolated audit phases and is still dominated by conventional IT-centric perspectives. Objectives: This paper systematically analyses recent advances in Agentic AI, Reinforcement Learning (RL), Large Language Models (LLMs), and tool-augmented Generative AI for autonomous VAPT. It aims to synthesise how these paradigms support end-to-end security auditing, identify the principal technical, operational, and governance gaps in the literature, and derive an evidence-grounded reference model for trustworthy autonomous auditing across both IT and OT environments. Methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted across major scholarly databases, covering publications from 2020 to 2025. From 1144 initially identified records, 72 studies were retained after deduplication, screening, and full-text eligibility assessment. Included studies were coded across five attributes and synthesised into thematic trajectories to derive the proposed framework. Study credibility was screened against three qualitative, non-instrumented criteria—venue and editorial process, presence of empirical or systematic conceptual evaluation, and explicit acknowledgement of limitations. Results: The review shows that agentic approaches are best suited to sequential and adaptive tasks such as reconnaissance orchestration, exploit-path selection, lateral movement, post-exploitation pivoting, and adaptive re-testing. In contrast, generative approaches are strongest in reasoning over unstructured evidence, interpreting configurations and advisories, contextualising vulnerabilities, assessing exploit feasibility, mapping compliance controls, and producing traceable audit reports. However, few studies integrate these capabilities into a governed end-to-end workflow, and real-world OT/Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) validation remains limited. Of the 72 coded studies, 56 apply classical machine or deep learning, 14 use generative/LLM techniques, and only 2 employ reinforcement-learning or agentic control; none is evaluated against a physical or emulated OT/IIoT target, and reported autonomy is strongly scaffolding-dependent (for example, 21% fully autonomous versus 64% human-assisted task completion on AutoPenBench, an external benchmark outside the coded corpus). To address these gaps, this paper derives a unified Agentic–Generative VAPT model comprising four tightly coupled layers: agentic decision-making, generative reasoning, structured tool interfaces, and validation–governance. It further introduces a formal threat and evaluation abstraction for Model Context Protocol (MCP)-style interface layers and proposes a five-dimensional VAPT Autonomy Benchmark for future empirical validation. Conclusion: Autonomous security auditing is evolving from isolated AI-assisted tasks towards integrated, policy-constrained, and auditable architectures. Nevertheless, major challenges remain in hallucination control, prompt injection, sparse reward design, explainability, safety-aware evaluation, and benchmark standardisation. Future research should prioritise tightly integrated agentic–generative systems, realistic and safety-aware IT/OT testbeds, and governance mechanisms that enable trustworthy human-in-the-loop deployment in operational environments.

items.title: AI for Technical Debt Management: Summary from the AI4TD Workshop at XP2026
items.abstract: Abstract Modern agile development and time-to-market pressures often lead to significant hidden technical debt (TD), which must be managed for sustainable software delivery. The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) for code generation can further increase TD if applied improperly. At the same time, software processes are becoming increasingly data-driven. This creates an opportunity: using AI to enable data-driven TD management in agile environments. This workshop offers a platform for researchers and practitioners to share ideas, experiences, and future visions on applying AI for TD management in agile development. The workshop was held in a half day and it consisted of three phases informing each other: (1) scientific talks (i.e., two paper presentations and two keynotes) that framed current challenges and their relevance; (2) two industrial talks shaping these problems in practice; and interactive sessions (i.e., group discussions and a fish bowl panel) that allowed participants to reflect about the current status of AI with respect to TD and next steps. These discussions define a research agenda that spans measurement, practices, education, and legacy modernization, and call for tight collaboration between industry and academia to keep pace with AI-augmented software development.

items.title: AI Use, Work-Life Balance, and Innovative Work Behavior as Predictors of Teacher Performance: The Mediating Role of Organizational Citizenship Behavior
items.abstract: Teachers are expected to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) effectively into instruction to enhance performance as agents of technological transformation in the Society 5.0 era. Previous studies showed ambiguous results regarding the role of AI in teacher performance and paid little attention to the behavioral mechanisms of the influence of technological, personal, and innovative aspects. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the impact of AI, work-life balance (WLB), and innovative work behavior (IWB) on teacher performance, with organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) serving as a mediator. A quantitative design was adopted through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyze data from 200 teachers in North Sumatra Province, Indonesia, sampled using a purposive sampling method. The results showed that AI had no significant direct effect on teacher performance (β = 0.112, p = .087), while WLB (β = 0.290, p < .001) and IWB (β = 0.110, p = .007) had a significant and positive effect. Furthermore, OCB mediated the relationship between AI, WLB, IWB, and teacher performance significantly. This study contributed to the literature on the management of education and organizational behavior by identifying that OCB was a critical behavioral mechanism transforming technological, psychological, and innovative resources into high teacher performance.

items.title: AI vs. AI: An AI-Enabled Conversational Intervention to Inoculate Against AI-Generated Fake News
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is a double-edged sword that can be used to amplify the proliferation of highly sophisticated fake news as well as to fight it. In this work, we explore a new route: using one AI to inoculate humans against fake news generated by another AI. Motivated by psychological inoculation theory, we created ‘Alex’, a conversational AI agent that engages users in an adaptive conversational dialogue designed to build cognitive resilience against AI-generated, AI-related fake news. We tested its efficacy in a Solomon four-group experiment with 542 participants. The results of a 2 × 2 ANOVA show a significant main effect of the intervention on participants’ discrimination of true and false headlines, with no significant evidence of pretest sensitization. We show that AI can be designed as a scalable, interactive conversational intervention for delivering psychological inoculation against AI-generated, AI-related fake news.

items.title: AI-Augmented Agile Teams: A Research Agenda and Summary of the Human-AI Collaboration Workshop
items.abstract: Abstract Agile teams are rapidly adopting AI agents in everyday work, reporting increased productivity and faster feedback cycles. Simultaneously, the integration of AI raises new socio-technical issues concerning coordination, trust, roles, quality, and governance. To better understand these challenges, we organized the first International Human–AI Collaboration in Agile Teams workshop at XP 2026, with more than 40 participants from academia and industry. This paper reports on the outcomes of the workshop, synthesizing insights from interactive group discussions and collaborative analysis. The findings highlight how AI reshapes agile teamwork and workflows, introducing new human–AI collaboration patterns, shifting skills and roles, and raising challenges related to leadership, governance, and value assessment. A key emerging concept is cognitive debt, referring to the gradual loss or weakening of shared understanding in teams relying on AI-generated outputs. Based on these findings, we present a research agenda structured around eight key themes, including teamwork, workflows, autonomy, skills, value measurement, and adoption practices. The results emphasize that integrating AI into agile software development teams is not only a technical challenge but a socio-technical transformation requiring new practices, competencies, and organizational support.

items.title: AI-Driven Dynamic Trust in Zero Trust Architecture: A Systematic Literature Review of Machine Learning, Federated Learning and Governance Challenges
items.abstract: Sophisticated cyber threats have exposed the limits of perimeter-based security models, and Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) has increasingly been adopted as an alternative paradigm. Purpose: This Systematic Literature Review examines the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) within Zero Trust frameworks, covering dynamic trust scoring, behavioural analytics and federated learning, the latter treated as one strand of AI rather than a separate paradigm. Following PRISMA 2020, 22 studies published between 2022 and 2025 were identified across IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, MDPI and Nature/Scientific Reports, appraised against a five-criterion quality instrument and synthesised narratively. The studies included are few and heterogeneous, and their findings should be read accordingly. Ensemble and hybrid designs predominate (14 of 22). Twelve studies report quantitative results, of which only eight evaluate on real named datasets; reported accuracies of 95 to 99 per cent come from different datasets, tasks, threat models, and evaluation settings, and are neither directly comparable nor a field-level benchmark. Only three studies directly compare learned adaptive trust against a static rule-based baseline. No study reports live operational deployment. We identify thirteen technique categories, eleven implementation barriers, and seven emerging trends. This paper proposes an integrated eight-component framework for AI-driven dynamic trust management, along with a five-domain research agenda. The framework is conceptual and synthesis-derived and requires empirical validation before operational use.

items.title: AIM VR: Collaborative Decision Architecture in Immersive Space
items.abstract: AIM VR is a conceptual framework for a collaborative immersive environment based on the Atlas Insight Method (AIM), developed by Miho Osawa. The proposed environment enables multiple participants to observe, explore, and compare the structures underlying human judgment within a shared three-dimensional space. Decision premises, information, relationships, constraints, emotions, external factors, and alternative pathways are represented as interconnected spatial structures. Unlike conventional decision-support systems that primarily present recommendations or optimized solutions, AIM VR emphasizes human agency and the continuous evolution of decision structures through human choice. Participants can examine multiple decision pathways, exchange different perspectives, and make decisions according to their respective responsibilities and decision-making authority. Once a choice is made, the virtual decision structure is dynamically reconstructed to represent updated conditions, relationships, and constraints. New decision pathways then emerge, enabling participants to continue observing, discussing, comparing, and choosing. This process can be repeated as circumstances and decisions evolve. The conceptual design is connected to the six stages of Atlas Insight Method: Awareness → Insight → Structure → Translation → Integration → Momentum. AIM VR is intended to support individual and collective judgment without transferring decision-making authority to artificial intelligence. The concept was publicly introduced by Miho Osawa on November 29, 2025. This presentation documents the further visual development of the AIM VR concept in October 2026. AIM VR is envisioned as an immersive interface for observing decision architecture through embodied spatial experience. Rather than merely viewing decision structures on a screen, participants enter a shared three-dimensional environment where relationships, constraints, and evolving decision pathways can be experienced spatially. The objective is not to automate judgment, but to extend human perception of the structures through which judgment emerges. AIM VR remains at the conceptual design stage. The system has not been implemented or empirically validated. The visual illustrations are AI-assisted conceptual representations intended to communicate the proposed immersive experience and structural design principles.

items.title: Antes do prompt: formulação de problemas e definição de objetivos no uso de inteligência artificial generativa por empreendedores
items.abstract: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools among entrepreneurs has been accompanied by a practical emphasis on writing prompts. This theoretical essay argues that this emphasis diverts attention from an earlier and more consequential step: formulating the problem and defining the outcome one seeks to achieve. We distinguish two patterns of use. In task-first use, the entrepreneur asks the AI for an immediate deliverable (a text, a plan, an analysis) without making explicit the goal it serves. In outcome-first use, the entrepreneur first states the desired outcome, diagnoses the problem, defines success criteria and constraints, and only then delegates tasks to the AI. We integrate four bodies of literature: research on problem finding and problem formulation, goal-setting theory, research on entrepreneurial decision-making under uncertainty (effectuation, the scientific approach, and experimentation), and recent empirical evidence on productivity, human–AI collaboration, and overreliance on automation. Building on this integration, we propose a conceptual model of pre-prompt problem formulation, with mechanisms (goal fit, calibrated evaluation, and selective implementation) and boundary conditions (task structure, position relative to the AI capability frontier, degree of uncertainty, and the entrepreneur's baseline performance), and we derive eight propositions. We discuss implications for individual entrepreneurs, limitations of the argument, and a research agenda that includes a three-arm field experiment. The article presents no empirical data; its propositions are intended for testing.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND INCLUSION: RETHINKING TEACHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: This theoretical article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can contribute to teacher education in Francophone Africa in support of inclusive education. Drawing on a critical synthesis of academic literature and institutional frameworks, it analyses AI’s potential to support differentiated instruction, the transformation of teachers’ professional roles, and the ethical, linguistic and infrastructural challenges associated with its adoption. It proposes a four-dimensional teacher-education model comprising technological, pedagogical, ethical and contextual dimensions. AI can support the personalization of learning, provided that teachers retain professional responsibility and that inequalities of access, local languages and educational realities are taken into account. The proposed model offers a conceptual framework for critical and context-sensitive integration of AI and requires empirical validation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence based human resource analytics and sustainability driven employee job performance through the mediating role of employee engagement in the information technology sector
items.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Management has changed how organizations analyse workforce information and support HR decision-making, creating new opportunities to strengthen sustainable employee performance. This study examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence-Based Human Resource Analytics (AI-HRA) and Sustainability-Driven Employee Job Performance (SDEJP), while also investigating the mediating role of Employee Engagement among employees in the Information Technology industry. The study is primarily grounded in Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) Theory, while the Resource-Based View (RBV) provides a complementary perspective by viewing AI-HRA as an organizational capability. Data were collected from 350 IT employees, of whom 69.4% were male ( n = 243) and 30.6% were female ( n = 107), and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 3. The findings indicate significant positive relationships between AI-HRA and both Employee Engagement and SDEJP. Employee Engagement also has a significant positive relationship with SDEJP and partially mediates the relationship between AI-HRA and SDEJP. The measurement and structural models demonstrate acceptable levels of reliability, validity, predictive relevance, and model fit. The present research contributes to the growing body of evidence on artificial intelligence-enhanced human resource management by linking an organizational AI-HRA capability with employee-level engagement and sustainable job performance. In practice, the results emphasize the significance of adopting AI-based human resource analytics alongside employee engagement interventions for sustainable employee performance and interpreted as positive associations within the sampled context rather than as evidence that AI-HRA automatically improves employee outcomes.

items.title: Association of generative artificial intelligence use with perceived academic benefit and reported performance among medical students
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are widely adopted by medical students. Although student attitudes toward AI have been surveyed extensively, far less is known about whether students who use these tools more often also report better academic outcomes. This study asked whether AI usage frequency is associated with perceived academic benefit and with self-reported academic performance among medical students at a single institution. A cross-sectional survey was administered to medical students at a single U.S. allopathic medical school. Students reported AI usage frequency, perceived academic benefit (composite of three Likert-scale items; Cronbach’s α = 0.84), self-reported overall exam performance, and self-rated academic standing. Spearman correlations with 95% confidence intervals and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used to examine associations. Of 103 respondents, students who used AI more frequently reported significantly greater perceived academic benefit (ρ = 0.69, 95% CI [0.57, 0.78], P < 0.001). However, AI usage frequency was not correlated with self-reported exam performance (ρ = −0.02, P = 0.81) or self-rated academic standing (ρ = −0.01, P = 0.93). Over half of students (53.4%) reported using AI Often or Always for studying. In this exploratory single-institution study, students who used AI more frequently perceived greater academic benefit, but this perception was not reflected in coarse, self-reported performance measures. This discrepancy should be interpreted cautiously and is at least as likely to reflect a measurement artifact, arising from the insensitivity of a single global performance item, recall bias, and the inability to distinguish performance before and after AI adoption, as a true gap between perception and attainment. Findings underscore the importance of helping medical students critically evaluate their AI-assisted study practices and identify priorities for more rigorous future investigation using objective, granular performance outcomes.

items.title: AURA - AI POWERED ADAPTIVE LEARNING
items.abstract: Most online courses give every learner the same lessons at the same pace, so gaps in understanding often go unnoticed. This presents AURA (AI-Powered Adaptive Learning System), a web application that generates a course from a learner’s goal and adapts it to the learner’s quiz results. A large language model (LLM) creates a course outline with modules, lessons, topics and prerequisite links, and each lesson is written when the learner opens it. A tutor based on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers questions from the current lesson and cites the passages it used. After each multiple-choice quiz, a weighted moving average updates a mastery score and a confidence value for the topic, and fixed rules select the next step and the next quiz difficulty. All LLM output is validated against schemas. In a pilot run with the gpt-5.4-mini model, five of seven generation jobs succeeded on the first attempt without repair. Two failed, one because of a provider quota error and one because the safety-check output was invalid. A course outline and first lesson were ready in 26.6 s. The prototype supports multiple-choice questions only, uses fixed adaptation rules and has not been tested with real learners.

items.title: Automated Confirmation Bias-Epistemic Laundering and Sycophancy in Statutory AI Decision-Making
items.abstract: Recent operational deployments of Large Language Models (LLMs) within public safety and statutory decision-making frameworks—highlighted by active misconduct investigations into police deployment of generative AI—expose a critical vulnerability in information governance and data integrity. This paper formalises the concept of "epistemic laundering": the mechanism by which Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) optimisation creates structural sycophancy, causing LLMs to extract subtle, unconscious human bias and transform it into authoritative institutional record. When deployed in decision-justification, risk-assessment, or investigative roles, these systems do not provide objective analytical rigour; instead, they function as automated confirmation engines that corrupt the evidentiary record. By disarming human critical verification through fluent, polished output, sycophantic models induce severe automation bias, leading to the total breakdown of information governance controls and human-in-the-loop verification. Applying formal information management principles, this paper evaluates these failure modes and proposes strict domain boundaries and record-keeping protocols to protect statutory data integrity. Keywords: Epistemic laundering, large language models, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), sycophancy, information governance, statutory decision-making, audit boundary, automation bias.

items.title: Bridging Capability and Conscience: A Pedagogical Framework for AI Literacy, Ethics, and Equity in Modern Education
items.abstract: The widespread expansion of adaptive algorithms and generative artificial intelligence across learning environments calls for an urgent re-evaluation of digital competency criteria. Conventional frameworks for technological literacy tend to prioritise mechanical execution—such as software operation, prompt engineering, and productivity gains. Although artificial intelligence offers diverse pedagogical utilities, including personalised study portals, automated grading mechanisms, and facial analysis tools for monitoring student behaviour, the societal and ethical fallout of these deployments is rarely addressed within K-12 settings. This study introduces a comprehensive educational model that merges technical aptitude, practical ethics, and systemic fairness. By synthesising current literature, empirical implementation studies, and international benchmarks (including the UNESCO AI Competency Frameworks for Students and Teachers), this paper pinpoints severe vulnerabilities in existing educational rollouts: systemic algorithmic bias, data privacy exploitation, cognitive erosion, and widening socioeconomic digital divides. Finally, it outlines an applied three-stage structural model—Understand, Scrutinise, and Equitable Creation—designed to transition educators and students from passive technology consumers into ethical assessors and active co-creators.

items.title: Closed-Loop Reinforcement Learning in De Novo Molecular Design: Bridging Generative AI with Automated Chemical Synthesis
items.abstract: Closed-loop reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to integrating generative molecular design with automated chemical synthesis and experimental evaluation. However, translating autonomous chemical optimization into pharmaceutical discovery remains challenging because biological measurements are often delayed, variable, and affected by assay limitations. This critical review and perspective examines current autonomous discovery platforms and evaluates the challenges associated with incorporating physical experimental feedback into molecular optimization. It proposes an uncertainty-aware, multi-objective reward architecture and a four-gate qualification framework covering operational synthesizability, analytical identity and purity, biological assay validity, and governed policy updating. Particular attention is given to distinguishing statistically censored measurements from pharmacologically confounded or invalid observations. The article also introduces supervised autonomy as a practical governance approach in which automated systems perform routine experimental operations while scientific experts retain responsibility for critical decisions. The proposed framework provides a foundation for improving the reliability, interpretability, and practical implementation of experimentally informed molecular discovery. Prospective validation remains necessary to establish its effectiveness.

items.title: Cognitive Conflict and Critical Thinking Skills in Science Education: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Critical thinking is an essential competency in science education because it enables students to analyze information, evaluate evidence, draw inferences, and make reasoned decisions. Cognitive conflict—arising when students’ prior conceptions encounter information or phenomena inconsistent with their existing understanding—may provide opportunities to reconsider explanations and examine evidence. This review examines (1) how cognitive conflict strategies have been designed and implemented to support critical thinking in science education, (2) how critical thinking has been operationalized and assessed, and (3) opportunities and challenges associated with integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and adaptive learning. The study uses a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with narrative synthesis. Sixteen articles were mapped for the period October 10, 2016–October 10, 2026. The mapped literature includes studies on cognitive conflict in physics education, instructional media development, critical thinking assessment, conceptual change, and GenAI use. The preliminary synthesis indicates that cognitive conflict has been integrated into inquiry learning, discovery learning, interactive multimedia, e-books, augmented reality, and educational websites. However, only a small subset of the mapped studies directly measured critical thinking, while others focused on conceptual understanding, misconception remediation, scientific literacy, creativity, or product development. The GenAI literature provides contextual insights into personalization and the risk of reduced cognitive engagement, but does not establish the effectiveness of integrating GenAI with cognitive conflict in physics education. The review identifies a need to align cognitive conflict activities with measurable critical thinking indicators and to evaluate GenAI as a scaffold.

items.title: Developers as Managers of AI Agents: A Workplace Shadowing Study
items.abstract: As AI coding agents become more autonomous, developers increasingly direct, coordinate, and check their work. Yet little is known about these practices in everyday professional development. We shadowed 11 professional developers across approximately 15 hours of work, coded their activities and task transitions, analyzed 255 submitted prompts, and conducted 4.6 hours of follow-up interviews. Developers spent an average of 33.4% of observed time formulating prompts or checking AI responses, with task-switching rates ranging from 0 to 101.6 switches per hour. Beyond producing artifacts, prompts supported understanding, requirements clarification, agent configuration, and coordination. We identified three recurring patterns: \textit{Supervisor}, involving direct artifact inspection; \textit{Delegator}, involving dialogue-based coordination and delegated implementation and checking; and \textit{Learner}, involving agents primarily to build understanding. Developers sought technical information from agents and organizational context, authority, and alignment from colleagues. Our findings suggest future studies of how developers manage attention across concurrent agent tasks and tools that support verification, coordination, and learning.

items.title: Digital Constitutionalism and the Protection of Fundamental Rights in the Age of AI: Rethinking Privacy, Equality and Freedom of Expression
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now decides who receives police protection and who gets government benefits and who gets employment or credit approval and who gets their online content promoted or deleted. The academic research and legal regulations that follow treat the resulting privacy violations and the breaks of equality and the restrictions on free speech as different issues. The paper presents three interrelated elements which demonstrate their relationship through three specific aspects: surveillance and profiling drive people to stop talking then automated content control systems create unfair distribution of when users speak and finally data practices which privacy legislation aims to control lead to unfair scoring outcomes. The study employs doctrinal and comparative approaches to examine three questions: (1) Do Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Indian Constitution provide sufficient protection against AI-related harms (2) What are the strengths and weaknesses of European Union and United States regulations governing AI systems used by public and private organizations (3) What protective measures should India implement. The Indian constitutional doctrine demonstrates strong power but the Indian legal system fails to provide sufficient support for automated decision-making and State exemptions and private-sector discrimination and remedies. The system establishes a comprehensive framework that consists of four hierarchical levels which include constitutional and legislative and institutional and remedial components. The law is stated as at 19 October 2026.

items.title: Digital-Based Career Counseling in the Era of Revolusi Industri 4.0 : Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The Industrial Revolution 4.0 has significantly transformed various aspects of human life, particularly in education and employment, through the integration of digital technology, artificial intelligence, big data, and the Internet of Things. These rapid changes demand new competencies such as digital literacy, critical thinking, adaptability, and career flexibility. In response to these challenges, digital-based career counseling has emerged as a strategic innovation to support students’ career development and readiness for the modern workplace. This study employs a literature review approach by analyzing recent national and international scientific publications indexed in Sinta, Scopus, and Google Scholar within the last five years. The analysis focuses on key themes including theoretical foundations, implementation models, benefits, and challenges of digital career counseling. The findings indicate that integrating classical career theories, such as Holland’s RIASEC personality typology and Super’s life-span, life-space theory, with digital platforms enhances accessibility, efficiency, and personalization of counseling services. Digital tools such as video conferencing, learning management systems, online assessments, and social media platforms contribute to improving career adaptability, career optimism, and employability skills among students. However, challenges remain in terms of counselors’ digital competence, ethical considerations, data security, and maintaining emotional connection in virtual interactions. Therefore, successful implementation of digital-based career counseling requires collaboration among government institutions, educational organizations, and technology developers to ensure effective, ethical, and student-centered services in the era of the Industrial Revolution 4.0.

items.title: Does Agentic AI Thin Out Entry-Level Employment? A Pre-Registered Test Using the Age Structure of U.S. Occupations, 2019–2026
items.abstract: This registration fixes, before the relevant outcome data are accessed, the hypotheses, data, variables, models and decision rules for a test of whether agentic AI systems accelerate the decline of early-career employment inside AI-exposed U.S. occupations. Between 2019 and 2024, occupations more exposed to large language models saw a larger fall in the share of workers aged 20–34, while their total employment did not fall (Thalassinidis & Bowen, The Price of Judgment, in preparation). Agentic systems, which carry out multi-step workflows and shift human work toward oversight and verification, may speed up this pattern. Using annual American Community Survey microdata (2019 and 2021–2026, with a pre-specified update for 2027), the primary test asks whether the relationship between occupational AI exposure and the early-career share bends more steeply after 2024 than its 2019–2024 trend, in a state-by-occupation panel. Secondary tests compare the agentic period with the generative-AI years alone (2022–2024), and examine whether any acceleration is larger in lower-consequence occupations and where agentic AI use is observed in API traffic. We also test that total employment is not affected. Only the 2019 and 2024 ACS data had been accessed at registration. The full plan, power simulation and data-access statement are attached. A companion preprint is posted on EdArXiv: https://osf.io/preprints/edarxiv/4a3vc_v1 (pending moderation at the time of registration).

items.title: Explainable AI for Fraud Alert Review in Community Banks and Credit Unions: A Narrative Review of Architectures, Analyst Workflows, and Governance
items.abstract: Community banks and credit unions face the same fraud schemes as large banks, but with far fewer analysts and data scientists. Machine-learning detectors help, yet an alert that gives no reason leaves the analyst to reconstruct the logic by hand, which slows investigations and complicates regulatory examinations. This narrative review looks at how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is being applied to fraud alerts in small financial institutions. Drawing on six recent sources, we trace the shift from rule-based systems to machine learning, describe architectural patterns that place an explanation layer between a detection model and the analyst, and discuss how explanations may shorten investigations, support analyst feedback, and strengthen model governance. One study reports that pairing ensemble anomaly detection with XAI reduced average analysis time from 4.2 hours to 35 minutes; we treat this as a single, unreplicated result. The evidence base is small, relies on single studies, and includes working papers and journals of uneven rigor, and it offers no shared benchmarks or analyst-centred evaluations. We close with practical implications for small institutions and open questions for future research.
